newsitem.title: USA: OMB's Raines sees no urgency to deal with CPI bias.
newsitem.headline: OMB's Raines sees no urgency to deal with CPI bias.

text.p: Franklin Raines, director of the Office of Management and Budget, said Friday that the issue of the consumer price index bias was complex, and that the administration was in no hurry to reach a decision on how to deal with it.

Speaking with reporters following remarks to a state legislators group, Raines also said it was possible that with the help of a strong economy the U.S. budget deficit this year could come in below the $107 billion red ink in fiscal 1996.
During his remarks, the OMB director made clear that the budget presented by the president would lead to balance and there was no need to tinker with it.
Raines said that if the Republicans were unwilling to deal with the president's budget offering they should produce their own so that work could begin.
He also told the legislators group that the data released earlier today showing job creation of 339,000 last month reflected a "sound fiscal policy and a monetary policy that complemented" it.

He also made clear during his discussion with reporters that the strong jobs data suggested that the economy was doing well, and that this could reduce the budget deficit further than estimates since additional revenues would be coming in.
The administration in its formal budget forecast a deficit for this year of $125 billion, and the Congressional Budget Office had come up with a figure of $112 billion, according to Raines.
But he said the actual figure, buoyed by a good economy, could show an improvement on both these estimates.

Raines also made clear that the administration felt no urgency to make a final decision on how to deal with the CPI bias and that it was seeking advice from experts in order to come up with a proper approach.
"There are people who are saying a variety of things," Raines told reporters. "If there was a common view, then we would be doing it, (but) it turns out there is no common view."
Raines added that, "We'll get where we're going at the proper time, but we're not feeling somehow that we've got to rush."
